area.description: This should be only about geometry in the tradition of Euclid, i.e., about lines, points, angles, circles, etc. If merely a 3D object is used, that is not enough (e.g., a 'tetrahedron' could be used just for its graph-theoretic properties of vertices and edges—which has nothing to do with its 3D geometry).
High school math competition algebra. Almost all problems involving real numbers should have this tag.
This should be only about geometry in the tradition of Euclid, i.e., about lines, points, angles, circles, etc.
Algebraic problems about the trigonometric functions.

This tag is mutually exclusive with the tags 'Geometry' and '3D Geometry'. Example terms: convex hulls, packings, tessellations, topology, etc. Make sure that the problem does not fall under (synthetic) geometry; e.g., if it deals with lengths, angles, areas, collinearity, concyclic points, etc., then it's likely a better fit for 'Geometry' or '3D Geometry'. Also, if a problem is tagged with this, it should also fall under the area of 'Combinatorics' (though it shouldn't be tagged as such, due to being less specific).
A broad area: high school math competition combinatorics. This includes, but is not limited to, games, problems on grids, graphs, permutations, tilings, puzzles, etc.
Problems that are purely about logic, i.e., there is no underlying theory (it's not about numbers, not about geometry—just pure logic).

Associated with natural numbers/integers, divisibility, rationality/irrationality, etc. The presence of integers alone is NOT enough — let the goal decide. Choose Number Theory only when the goal is genuinely number-theoretic (e.g. proving a value is a perfect square, divisible, or itself an integer), even when posed as an algebraic equation. If the goal is to count or to maximize the size of a set, it is Combinatorics; if to prove an inequality, it is Algebra — even when the objects are integers.

goal.description: The objective is to prove equivalence of two propositions. This is usually more specific than 'Prove General Statement', so use only this tag if both are applicable.
The objective is to prove the existence of some object. The proof need not necessarily be a constructive one (i.e. proving existence without actually constructing one such object is fine).
The objective is to prove that there is exactly one solution.
The objective is to prove that no object satisfies the property.
The objective is to prove that certain objects satisfy some property.
The objective is to find out if there is a solution -- i.e. either prove that a solution exists, or prove that a solution does not exist, for suitably defined 'solution'.

The task is to construct some geometric object (e.g., a point with some properties) using only certain tools (e.g., compass and straightedge). Implies the area tag 'Geometry' or '3D Geometry'. Prefer this over 'Find Solution' if applicable.

The objective is to construct some object (it is not enough to merely prove existence). This is more specific than 'Prove Existence', so use only this tag if both are applicable. Do not award this if 'Geometric Construction' could be awarded.

The objective is to find out if there is a solution, and if there is a solution, find one. This can only be applied to problems where it is not clear whether a solution exists. This is more specific than the tag 'Does Solution Exist?' so use only this tag if both are applicable.

Problem where we are looking for a 'best' / minimal / maximal solution according to some metric. For example, in combinatorics, it could be about the smallest number of steps to reach some outcome. In algebra, it could be about minimizing some formula. This is more specific than 'Find Solution' (since we are asking for best solution, whereas in constructive problems we are asking only for some solution) -- so if both are applicable, use only this tag.
The objective is to either prove that certain objects satisfy some property, or find a counterexample.

The objective is to find the number of solutions (we do not actually have to find the solutions themselves, just their number). This includes problems where we are to place an upper or lower bound on the number of solutions. Make sure that the count is the count of solutions (and not count of something else).

The objective is, given a game (usually with 2 players), prove that a certain player can play such that they cannot lose, no matter what the other players are doing. Implies the area tag 'Combinatorics' or 'Combinatorial Geometry'.

The objective is, given a game (usually with 2 players), determine which player has the winning strategy / prove that a given player has a winning strategy. Implies the area tag 'Combinatorics' or 'Combinatorial Geometry'.
The objective is to find all solutions, for suitably defined 'solutions'. For example it could be something like 'determine all possible values of some property / variable X'.

E.g. calculate the length / circumference / angle / ... Use this only when the problem asks us directly to calculate some value where it is *not immediately obvious how to calculate it*. It must be clear from the problem statement that the value is uniquely determined and that the hard part is calculating it from known information.

type.description: This should be assigned only to problems that explicitly deal with the absolute value function (and not as a vector/segment length indicator). Do not assign this just because the problem involves a (positive) difference.
This should be assigned only to problems that involve filling in missing digits into given cells to make a sum work. Do not assign this just because there are digits in a problem.
Do not award this just because there are consecutive numbers in the statement; there must be an explicit mention of an arithmetic progression.
Use this only when the problem involves a non-decimal system. Since most problems are in decimal, this tag is generally not useful.
Only award this when the problem explicitly deals with divisibility.

Award only to combinatorial game problems — typically two players alternating moves (occasionally a solitaire process) — where the task is to determine a winning or drawing strategy, so the Goal is 'Winning Strategy' or 'Drawing Strategy'. Do not award just because the words 'game' or 'play' appear; there must be an actual game whose strategy is analyzed.
Use this tag when a problem involves a process that is being repeated.
Award this only when there is a binomial number in the problem explicitly; do not assume it is in the solution.
Use this if the problem involves a lattice or some other kind of regular grid.
This tag is for problems where the goal is to prove an inequality or to find the maximum or minimum of an expression. Do not award this tag just because there is some sort of an inequality sign.
Award only to problems where we explicitly deal with either a periodic sequence or are proving that a sequence is periodic.

Award only to problems that deal with a permutation of a sequence of objects. Do not award just because a problem involves determining an order of something; the word 'order' alone is not enough. Pairing or partitioning a set into pairs or groups is a matching, not a permutation.

Award only to geometry problems where we are proving that something passes through a fixed point, or (rarely) to algebra problems that explicitly deal with numbers t such that f(t) = t or something similar.

Use this tag only if the polynomial mentioned in the problem has an unknown or variable degree, or a degree of at least 3. Just having an expression is not enough for this tag, such as when merely minimizing an expression.

Award only to problems that are explicitly about a right triangle (one is given, or is the central object of the configuration). Do not award just because a right angle or perpendicular lines appear somewhere in the figure.
Here we mean an arithmetic or geometric mean, not a circle's diameter.
Use this tag only if the problem statement states the recurrence relation directly. If the recurrence is not immediately obvious, do not use this tag.

Be a bit stricter when awarding this tag. Just because there is a condition expressible or expressed as an equation does not mean you have to assign the equation tag. Reserve it for problems involving solving an equation, such as real-valued equations or Diophantine equations.
If the problem involves a square grid, use the 'Grid' tag instead of this one.

Use this tag when there is an explicit system of at least two simultaneous equations in the statement. A recurrence relation (a single equation parameterized over an index, defining a sequence) is NOT a system — use 'Recurrence Sequence' for that. Do not use both this tag and 'Equation'.
Award only to problems that mention this explicitly, i.e. the remainder after a division.

technique.description: Award only to problems that require an abstract usage of this theorem, i.e. when it is used to prove the existence of some number. Do not award just because we manually need to find such a problem in a special case.
Award only to problems that actually use this principle explicitly in their solution in a non-trivial way. Make sure it is truly a non-trivial and essential step in the solution.

Award only to problems that actually use this technique by explicitly assuming something is maximal or minimal. This is a very subtle technique and should only be awarded where such an assumption is an essential, nontrivial step in the solution - for example, as in the tricky solution to the Sylvester problem. Do not award this tag to problems that merely mention a minimum or maximum in their text or solution, especially not to those that simply ask to prove or determine when something is minimal or maximal.
Award only when the solution explicitly involves considering something which does not change. Do not award just because the problem contains a mention of a change.
Explicit mention in the solution is required.
Induction must be mentioned explicitly, not just implicitly by there being a process.

Award only when the problem involves a tricky, unobvious factorization, such as the Sophie Germain identity. Do not award this just because there is some factorization in a problem - in fact, most problems will have some. This tag is exclusively for tricky usages.
Explicit mention in the solution is required.

Explicit mention in the solution is required, not just there being a perpendicular angle bisector. We need an explicit usage of the fact that the bisector divides a side in the ratio of the other sides.
